wine.name: Rapsani Reserve
wine.classification: Reserve, Epilegmenos in Greek: at least two years of ageing under the Rapsani PDO
wine.grapes: Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto in roughly equal shares, the three grown side by side and fermented together.
wine.sites: Growers' vineyards on the south eastern slopes of Mount Olympus above the Vale of Tempe, at about 250 to 600 metres by the house's account, within sight of the Aegean.
wine.making: The three grapes were fermented together, as the appellation asks, in the house's own winery at Rapsani. A Reserve must be aged two years in all, at least twelve months in oak and six in bottle; by an importer's sheet the house gave it a year in French barrels of 300 litres, part new, and a year in bottle.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, dried plum and tomato leaf with leather, clove and a dusty, earthen note; medium bodied and fuller than a Naoussa, with Xinomavro's lively acidity and a tannin rounded by Krassato.
wine.ageing: It drank well from about five years after the vintage and a strong year held for a decade and more; the bottles met are old ones, so open them soon.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; stand an old bottle upright and decant it gently off its sediment; a Burgundy or Nebbiolo style glass.

records.table: Tsantali Rapsani Reserve was the Rapsani that carried the appellation abroad: Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto from the slopes of Mount Olympus, fermented together and aged a year in oak. The house stopped making wine in 2023, so the bottles met are older ones.
records.story: The Tsantali family began making wine and distilling tsipouro in 1890 at Sidirochori in Eastern Thrace. Evangelos Tsantalis (1913 to 1996) moved the business west, setting up a distillery at Thessaloniki in 1945, and wine became the house's main work. Rapsani, on the south eastern slopes of Mount Olympus, was made an appellation in 1971, yet its vineyards had fallen close to abandonment. Tsantali took up the zone, as its viticulturist told it, working with the local growers to save the old vines and to plant more, and made its Rapsani, its Reserve and its Grande Reserve from the three grapes fermented together in its own winery there. Until 2005, by the account of the Greek wine body, it was the appellation's only producer, and Rapsani owes its survival to it. The house stopped production in 2023, a court declared it bankrupt, and the bankruptcy was entered in the commercial registry on 12 January 2026. For a sommelier the Reserve is the Rapsani of a generation: the wine that taught the world the three grapes and the mountain.

report: The year Tsantali came to Rapsani is not settled: 1991 by one guide and the plan's thin run, the early 1980s by a GuildSomm article, so the story gives no year.

The closure: production stopped in August 2023 by Protothema and in September 2023 by PowerGame and SKAI, so the record says 2023; Parapolitika gives the court's decision as 1 December 2025, and Protothema and PowerGame the registry entry of 12 January 2026.

The Reserve's ageing terms are read from the Ministry's Rapsani file through a search summary (two years, at least twelve months in oak and six in bottle; the Grande Reserve four years); the Grande Reserve's eighteen months in oak is the importers', not the PDO's.

The founding of 1890 rests on Wines of Greece's Tsantali page and on Wikipedia, gtp.gr and wein-plus; Evangelos Tsantalis's dates and the move of 1945 rest on wein-plus and Wikipedia through search summaries.

Wines of Greece says Krassato and Xinomavro must each be at least a third of a Rapsani; Decanter says the shares are not fixed; the Codex's region record teaches equal thirds. The grapes field says roughly equal shares, as the importer gives this wine.
The house's work with the growers rests on one quoted remark of its viticulturist in GuildSomm, hedged as his account; GuildSomm also says the house owned no vines of its own at Rapsani.

wine.name: Rapsani Old Vines
wine.grapes: Xinomavro, the larger part, with Krassato and a little Stavroto from the same old vineyards.
wine.sites: Old bush vines of sixty years and more on poor, iron rich schist, high on the north eastern slopes of Mount Olympus above Rapsani, farmed organically and without irrigation.
wine.making: The three grapes are fermented together, as the appellation asks, and the wine is aged for eighteen months in French and American oak barrels, lightly toasted or not toasted at all so the wood stays behind the fruit, then six months in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Ripe red cherry, plum and dried tomato with black olive, clove and a stony, schist laid note; riper and rounder than a Naoussa, with Xinomavro's fresh acidity and firm, fine grained tannin.
wine.ageing: Generous within three or four years of the vintage; a strong year gains over a decade and more.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Burgundy or Nebbiolo style glass.

records.table: Dougos Rapsani Old Vines comes from bush vines of sixty years and more on the schist of Mount Olympus, farmed organically, with Xinomavro leading Krassato and Stavroto. Eighteen months in barrel give it a riper, rounder Xinomavro; decant it for an hour.
records.story: The Dougos family were nurserymen before they were winemakers: its vine nursery near Rapsani has propagated the local grapes, Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto among them, for some sixty years. Rapsani had been an appellation since 1971, but its vineyards were close to abandonment and one large house, Tsantali, made nearly all its wine. In the early 1990s, in 1991 by most accounts, the family set up a winery of its own at the foot of Mount Olympus, in the Tempi valley. Its vineyards, high on the mountain on poor schist, were turned over to organic farming and worked without irrigation. By the account of the Greek wine body, Tsantali was Rapsani's only producer until 2005; others followed after it, the family among them, and the appellation's own technical file names the house as making Rapsani from its own vineyard in the zone. A brother and sister of the next generation, a viticulturist and a chemist who makes the wine, carry it on. Old Vines, from the family's old bush vines, is the grower's answer to the large house: the same three grapes, from older vines, raised longer in wood.

wine.name: Rapsani
wine.grapes: Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto, the appellation's three grapes, fermented together.
wine.sites: The family's own vineyards around the village of Rapsani on the slopes of Mount Olympus, at about 200 to 550 metres by the house's account.
wine.making: The three grapes are fermented together with their own wild yeasts in the family's small winery, and the wine is then aged for twelve months in old oak barrels, which give it shape without the taste of new wood, before bottling.
wine.glass: Sour cherry and red plum with tomato leaf, black olive and a cool hint of eucalyptus; medium bodied, with Xinomavro's lively acidity and firm tannin softened by its two partners.
wine.ageing: Open within three or four years of the vintage; a strong year keeps for about a decade.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour; a Burgundy or Nebbiolo style glass.

records.table: The Liapis family's Rapsani is a grower's wine from the village itself: Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto fermented together with wild yeasts and given a year in old oak. Expect sour cherry, tomato leaf and olive, and pour it a touch cool.
records.story: The Liapis family have grown grapes at Rapsani for generations; by the house's own account their first family vineyard was planted in about 1935, on the slopes of Mount Olympus above the village. Rapsani was made an appellation in 1971, and by the Greek wine body's account Tsantali was the only producer in the zone until 2005. In 2002, as the house tells it, the founder's grandson, the third generation, took over the vineyards and set up a small, fully equipped winery to make the family's own wine. The Rapsani is its wine to know: the three grapes of the appellation fermented together with their own yeasts and aged a year in old oak, a village wine rather than a showpiece. The house is one of the stations on the Route of the Gods of Olympus, one of the wine routes of northern Greece, beside Tsantali, Dougos and Chrisohoou, and it has stood among the sponsors of Rapsani's August festival of wine and the vine. For a sommelier it is the grower's Rapsani, made in the village by a family that has farmed its vines for nearly a century.

wine.grapes: Xinomavro, about half, with Krassato and a smaller share of Stavroto.

records.table: Terra Petra is the Rapsani of Terra Olympus, the Mount Olympus company of the Naoussa house Thymiopoulos: Xinomavro, about half, with Krassato and Stavroto from steep schist slopes. It is supple and fresh, so pour it a little cool.
records.story: The Thymiopoulos family grew grapes for generations at Trilofos in Naoussa, and its first wine under the family name, Earth and Sky, came out in 2005. Its Naoussa is Xinomavro alone; across the plain of Thessaly, on the slopes of Mount Olympus, Rapsani asks for Xinomavro with two partners, Krassato and Stavroto, and had been an appellation since 1971. By the importer's account, the house's Rapsani company, Terra Olympus, was set up in 2015, when vineyards within the appellation came up for sale; more were bought in 2016. They are steep slopes at about 500 metres, on schist, between the mountain and the sea, with many old bush vines. Terra Petra, named for that stony ground, was reviewed as PDO Rapsani from its 2015 vintage by an Austrian magazine and a British one. It is sold under the Thymiopoulos name, and it brought the Naoussa house's way with Xinomavro, ripe but fresh, raised in large barrels, to a second appellation. For a sommelier it shows what Rapsani tastes like from a newer hand: the same three grapes, a lighter touch, and the mountain in the glass.

wine.name: Rapsani
wine.grapes: Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto in equal shares, by the house's own account.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards on the slopes of Mount Olympus at 150 to 550 metres, on slate, above the mouth of the Tempi valley.
wine.making: A classic red vinification with fifteen days on the skins, then twelve months in French and American oak barrels of 225 and 300 litres, a third of them new and the rest in their second and third use, and a further twelve months in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Red cherry, dried plum and tomato leaf with vanilla and clove from the oak and a savoury, leathery edge from Krassato; medium bodied, with Xinomavro's fresh acidity and firm tannin.
wine.ageing: Ready on release, two years after the vintage; a good year keeps for six to eight more.

records.table: The Chrisohoou family's Rapsani comes from a small winery at Rapsani's railway station, where the Tempi valley opens to the sea: equal parts Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto, a year in French and American oak and a year in bottle.
records.story: The Chrisohoou family have grown vines on the slopes of Mount Olympus for four generations, by their own account. Rapsani was made an appellation in 1971, and by the Greek wine body's account and the family's, Tsantali was the zone's only producer until 2005. The family's winery stands at Rapsani's railway station, at the mouth of the Tempi valley where it opens to the sea, a site it has worked since the late 1990s. The station itself opened in 1916 on the line through Tempi, under the name of the nearby village of Pyrgetos, and reopened rebuilt in 2008. From there the family makes two Rapsanis of the three grapes in equal shares, a plain red and a Special Edition, both raised in oak and in bottle before release. The winery is one of the stations on the Route of the Gods of Olympus, one of the wine routes of northern Greece, and it has been among the sponsors of Rapsani's festival of wine and the vine. It is a house known at home and little seen abroad, and its Rapsani is the appellation in its plain, village form.

others.note: The house's limited Rapsani, given three days of cold soaking before fermentation and longer in bottle; the 2009 was its first.

report: The house is active: its own site (rapsaniwine.gr) lists a Rapsani PDO red and a Special Edition, a 2024 municipal report places its winemaker at a wine tourism meeting, and it sponsored the 2019 festival; no recent merchant listing was found abroad.

Founded stays empty: 1880 is in a blog post of 2009 alone, at an address that seems to carry a person's name, and the house's own history page gives no year, only four generations and the station site from the late 1990s.

Spelling: the plan's Chrisohoou stays as the producer; the house writes Chrysochoou in Greek and chrisochoou in its addresses, so the prose keeps the plan's spelling and the label term gives both; the exact label wording was not seen.

The house's own page says the rules ask Krassato to be a third of the blend and gives equal shares; the Codex's region record agrees; Wines of Greece gives at least a third each of Krassato and Xinomavro.

The glass is written from the house's grapes and oak, not from a critic's note, and kept modest; the Special Edition's 2009 as its first rests on the house's 2009 announcement and a Master of Wine's note of 2020.
The station's dates (1916, 2008) rest on Wikipedia alone through search summaries, and are offered as setting only; the integrator may cut them.
